tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK FOR THE BUSHY BRUSH
tiles.details: Bushy bluestem is a tufted perennial with erect culms often about 75–150 cm in Kew GrassBase. Numerous crowded short flowering units make a broad, cottony terminal brush, unlike broomsedge's more separated spathe-held units. Texas Uvalde whole-clump and USGS flowering photographs show this gross architecture; a white head alone is not definitive.
tiles.short: Many short silky paired racemes crowd into a broad oblong crown

tiles.heading: 02 · PART THE SPATHES
tiles.details: Look within the fluffy mass for short paired racemes, commonly about 1.5–3 cm, partly subtended by small leafy spathes. The silky hairs arise prominently from rachis internodes and pedicels. A whole flowering head does NOT expose each spathe boundary or a measured raceme pair; obtain a connected specimen and 1-mm ruler before placing anatomy arrows.
tiles.short: Find paired 1–3 cm rames inside short leafy spathe-like sheaths

tiles.heading: 03 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: The actual ligule is a short ciliolate membrane at the inner blade–sheath junction; the USFS bushy bluestem treatment describes it at about 1 mm. Sheaths can be flattened/keeled and may carry hairs on their margins, but broomsedge can also have sheath hairs. Open BOTH margins and expose the true ligule beside a 1-mm scale. Existing photographs do not prove these microscopic features.
tiles.short: A short ciliate membrane, not merely long sheath-margin hairs

tiles.heading: 04 · FIND THE FERTILE SESSILE SPIKELET
tiles.details: Kew GrassBase describes a 3–4.5 mm fertile sessile spikelet; the USFS treatment gives about 3–4 mm. Its pedicelled partner is usually strongly reduced or absent, leaving a silky-haired pedicel. Separate the two firmer enclosing glumes: the lower has two lateral keels; the upper has one mid-keel and is awnless. Glumes approximately reach or exceed the enclosed florets. Do not arrow a hair tuft as a pedicelled spikelet.
tiles.short: Ripe sessile spikelet roughly 3–4.5 mm; partner reduced or absent

tiles.heading: 05 · LOCATE THE REAL LEMMA AWN
tiles.details: Inside the glumes is a sterile lower floret with a thin lemma and an upper fertile floret whose hyaline lemma has a bifid tip. A SINGLE slender awn arises from the notch (sinus) of the fertile lemma, about 10–20 mm in Kew GrassBase; the USFS account gives about 10–15 mm. The awn is not a glume extension. A detached, scaled fertile lemma and awn insertion are still missing.
tiles.short: One straight awn from the cleft fertile lemma, usually 10–20 mm

tiles.heading: 06 · CHECK THE LOCAL BLUESTEMS
tiles.details: Anatherum virginicum has more individually separated narrow spathe-held units, although sheath hairs overlap. Schizachyrium scoparium has distributed short silky racemes; Andropogon gerardi has stout exposed turkey-foot fingers; KR bluestem has longer slender clustered fingers. Historical Andropogon glomeratus var. pumilus photographs belong to separately accepted A. tenuispatheum, NOT this species: gallery panel 6 is OTHER-species comparison only. Never infer county-native PASS from the Uvalde photo.
tiles.short: Broad bushy brush ≠ broomsedge's separate units or little bluestem

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: BUSHY BLUESTEM (Anatherum glomeratum): the official USGS true var. glomeratus flowering closeup NOW illustrates dense brushes of many clustered short, pale-silky racemes and leafy upper sheaths. Compare broomsedge's more separate narrow spathe-sheathed racemes, big bluestem's open turkey-foot, and historical Hawaiian var. pumilus now under A. tenuispatheum. Confirm intact raceme pair, spathe and sessile/pedicellate spikelets under magnification; photo gross architecture alone is not specimen-proof.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: The actual ligule is a short ciliolate membrane at the inner blade–sheath junction; the USFS bushy bluestem treatment describes it at about 1 mm. Sheaths can be flattened/keeled and may carry hairs on their margins, but broomsedge can also have sheath hairs. Open BOTH margins and expose the true ligule beside a 1-mm scale. Existing photographs do not prove these microscopic features.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Kew GrassBase describes a 3–4.5 mm fertile sessile spikelet; the USFS treatment gives about 3–4 mm. Its pedicelled partner is usually strongly reduced or absent, leaving a silky-haired pedicel. Separate the two firmer enclosing glumes: the lower has two lateral keels; the upper has one mid-keel and is awnless. Glumes approximately reach or exceed the enclosed florets. Do not arrow a hair tuft as a pedicelled spikelet.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Bushy bluestem forms a densely crowded oblong tuft of many short silky paired racemes, each arising with a spathe-like bract. Broomsedge has more separated, narrower spathe-sheathed pairs; little bluestem has shorter individual silky racemes borne on distributed leafy upper branches; big bluestem has relatively stout digitate turkey-foot fingers; KR has more slender longer clustered fingers, not the dense tuft.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

memory_rule: BUSHY: MANY SILKY SHORT CLUSTERS packed into a dense crown. LOOK for true paired racemes in the spathes at macro scale; old Hawaiian var. pumilus images are NOT A. glomeratum.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
